text: This section synthesises the review of the 44 primary studies presented in Section 2.4 against the six requirements defined in Section 2.2. Across the corpus, the requirement that is most often satisfied is the representation of consent as an evaluable authorisation object (Req 1), which 14 studies satisfy fully and 30 satisfy in part. Policy- and context-aware enforcement (Req 4) is satisfied fully by 13 studies, in part by 25 and not at all by 6, and temporal validity and lifecycle control (Req 5) is satisfied fully by 8 studies, in part by 26 and not at all by 10. Decentralised verification of identity and authority (Req 2) is satisfied fully by 7 studies and in part by 35, and only 2 studies describe no identity mechanism at all. Multi-party authorisation through a verifiable threshold (Req 3) is the least satisfied requirement: 6 studies satisfy it fully, 4 satisfy it in part and 34 do not address it. With respect to Req 6, formal security assurance of the authorisation decision is provided by 6 studies and argued informally by 17, while 21 studies offer no security analysis beyond assertion; empirical validation is complete in 5 studies, partial in 35 and absent in 4. It should be noted that these proportions are consistent with the signal prevalence in the wider full-text pool of 1,805 records, in which only 8% of the records carry a multi-party signal, 2% a temporal-validity signal and 1% a formal-verification signal, compared with 74% for audit or evidence and 69% for a prototype or experiment. The scarcity observed among the included studies is therefore a property of the field and not an artefact of the selection.

The most important correction that the review imposes on the framing of this research concerns multi-party authorisation. An earlier version of this chapter, built on a smaller corpus, stated that multi-party authorisation of patient consent does not exist in the literature. That statement is withdrawn. The coding panel identified six distinct mechanism classes in which more than one party participates in an authorisation-related decision. Madine et al. [53] require regulator and guardian approvals on a single access request, but only on the incapacitated and emergency paths; on the normal path a single patient key authorises, so that joint approval is a contingency rather than a standing condition. Wu et al. [75] apply a (t, n) threshold of investigators, but the threshold governs the admission of a trial record to the ledger and the revocation of a consent rather than the grant, and the vote itself reduces to a hash-integrity check. Zhao and Su [50] place the threshold among consumer-side delegates who are already within the access policy, and Tan et al. [69] place it among patient-appointed witnesses who act for a patient who is unable to act. Punia et al. [61] conjoin an institutional M-of-N signature with an attribute policy, but the signature is reserved for high-sensitivity and cross-departmental requests, lies outside the decision predicate and can be bypassed by a single emergency officer. Ekholm et al. [43] and Hagström et al. [47] report deployed national platforms in which all legal guardians must co-sign at consent registration and guardianship is verified against a population register; the co-consent is a validity condition of the registered consent and not a predicate evaluated on each subsequent access request. In addition, Maruthi and Singh [54] distribute a threshold key among patient-designated relatives, and Abbasi et al. [35] among automated oracles, so that the threshold protects key custody rather than expressing an authorisation judgement. Therefore, multi-party approval exists in the reviewed literature as a contingency path, a registration-time co-consent, an institution-side admission gate, a custodial M-of-N, a witness or notary threshold, or a key-share reconstruction. In no reviewed study is it a constitutive predicate that every access decision must satisfy together with the identity, policy and temporal conditions, and in no study is the approving set both defined by the patient and evaluated on every request.

A similar qualification applies to Req 4 and Req 5. Purpose of use is evaluated inside the decision in several studies. Tith et al. [71] and Albalwy et al. [37] match a purpose tree or a purpose tuple, Jaiman and Urovi [49] match ontology terms, Román-Martínez et al. [63] evaluate the FHIR purpose-of-use through an XACML decision point, Eneh et al. [44] evaluate purpose, data category and jurisdiction in an on-chain rule set, and Panagoulias et al. [57] verify a purpose conjunct at scale. However, every one of these studies is single-party, and the one study that conjoins a policy engine with a multi-party signature, Punia et al. [61], carries no purpose term and consumes consent as a Boolean attribute. In the cryptographic schemes the policy is bound to the ciphertext or to the requester's attributes rather than to the consent [78, 46, 56], and in the deployed research infrastructures the purpose is displayed or logged rather than evaluated [72, 74, 73]. Purpose and data-scope policy that is bound to the consent object and conjoined with multi-party approval is therefore largely absent. Temporal enforcement inside the decision is rare. Eneh et al. [44] evaluate the validity bounds of a rule at request time, the key-derivation scheme in [64] binds the expiry into the key so that decryption after expiry is unreachable, Madine et al. [53] discount stale attestations, and Punia et al. [61] check token expiry on access. In most other studies the time element is a stored timestamp [37, 71], an expiry field that the decision algorithm never reads [58], a session or token lifetime rather than a consent validity window [73, 67, 51], or a claimed auto-expiry with no enforcement locus [68, 70]. Verified revocation with an observed denial is reported by Panagoulias et al. [57] and Phuyal et al. [58], and in a single narrated scenario in [68]; elsewhere revocation is specified and its cost measured, but its effect on a subsequent request is not exercised [61, 62, 60]. The gap under Req 5 is therefore not the absence of temporal mechanisms but the enforcement, at the consent object itself and verified at decision time, of the validity interval, revocation and state transitions in a multi-institution exchange.

Formal assurance of the authorisation decision is almost absent, and where it exists it is narrow. The six studies with a formal proof, Wu and Zhang [76], Zhao and Su [50], Maruthi and Singh [54], Mei et al. [55], Hancheng et al. [48] and Luo et al. [52], prove anonymity, unforgeability, confidentiality or revocation properties of a cryptographic gate over one or two conditions. None of them contains a theorem stating that access is granted only if a conjunction of identity, authority, policy, temporal and lifecycle conditions holds, because none of them implements such a conjunction. Conversely, the studies with the broadest decision predicates, Punia et al. [61], Madine et al. [53], Ferreira et al. [45], Phuyal et al. [58], Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66] and Panagoulias et al. [57], provide at most a threat table or a structured adversary model. Across the corpus, therefore, the breadth of the decision predicate and the strength of its assurance vary inversely, and no study occupies the position in which a broad predicate is formally proved. The empirical evidence shows the same pattern from the other side. Five studies report a complete empirical evaluation [37, 47, 49, 57, 58], and only Panagoulias et al. [57] and Phuyal et al. [58] verify ALLOW and DENY outcomes systematically, the former in a single-node simulation and the latter without adversarial tests. A larger group of studies builds and measures a decision path without verifying a single authorisation decision [61, 35, 65, 72, 78, 36]; Sawant and Gomes [65] run the broadest measurement campaign in the corpus and report no outcome for the access-control function that they formalise. When the formal and empirical halves of Req 6 are combined, eleven studies reach a tick in the combined column of the tables of Section 2.4, but no study combines a formal proof of its decision with a systematic empirical test of that decision.

Taken together, the review establishes two gaps rather than one. The first is a conjunction gap. Identity and authority verification, collective approval, purpose and data-scope policy, temporal validity and lifecycle control each exist in the literature, several of them in mature form, and a number of studies combine three or four of them in one design [58, 61, 45, 66, 57]. No study, however, conjoins identity, authority, threshold, policy, temporal and jurisdictional and lifecycle conditions in one decision predicate in which multi-party approval is a standing condition of every access decision and in which the patient, rather than an institution, defines the approving set. The second is an assurance gap. Where the conditions do co-exist they are neither proved nor tested as an authorisation decision, and where a proof exists it covers a fragment of the predicate. The proposed framework is positioned against these two gaps. The consent object C carries the guardian set G and the threshold N together with the identity, policy, temporal, jurisdictional and lifecycle components; the access decision is the conjunction of the corresponding predicates; and the conjunction, rather than any single component, is the object of both formal and empirical assurance. It should be noted that the framework is not positioned on the idea of an evaluable consent object, which the literature has provided since 2020 [71, 37], nor on the existence of a threshold mechanism, which the six classes above provide, but on the conjunction of the conditions and on the assurance of that conjunction.

title: Research Gaps in the Existing Studies from the Requirement Perspective

text: Gap 1 (Req 1): The strongest evaluable consent objects in the reviewed studies are the purpose-based tuple of Tith et al. [71], the ontology object of Albalwy et al. [37], the on-chain consent object of Phuyal et al. [58], the consent token of Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66], the rule structure of Eneh et al. [44] and the policy object of Panagoulias et al. [57]. Each of them carries a subset of the required components: Tith et al. [71] and Albalwy et al. [37] carry no temporal component, Eneh et al. [44] and Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66] carry no authority requirement beyond the single patient, and Phuyal et al. [58] store an expiry that the decision algorithm does not read. In the 30 studies coded as partial, the consent is a Boolean flag, a logged event or a status that is displayed rather than evaluated [36, 60, 65, 74], and in Punia et al. [61] the object that carries a lifecycle is the policy rather than the consent. What remains open is a consent object that represents the participating identities, the authority requirement including the guardian set and the threshold, the purpose and data scope, the validity interval, the jurisdiction, the lifecycle state and the evidence as separately evaluable components. This gap corresponds to research question RQ1 of Chapter 3.

Gap 2 (Req 2): The clearest separations of identity from authority are found in Ekholm et al. [43] and Hagström et al. [47], where guardianship is verified against a national population register independently of the eID login, in Phuyal et al. [58], where a licensing-body credential asserts role and scope of practice separately from the wallet identity, in Wu and Zhang [76], where a zero-knowledge proof binds the owner's authorisation to a specific requester key, and in Tan et al. [69], Madine et al. [53] and Tseng et al. [73]. In the 35 studies coded as partial the identity is a wallet address or a platform certificate, the role is administratively assigned or self-selected at login [36, 44], and the authority to act on behalf of a patient is not evidenced at all. The register-based guardian verification of [43, 47] is centralised, and the DID and VC designs [58, 45, 66] carry no guardian credential. What remains open is decentralised evidence of both identity and authority for every participant in a consent, including the guardians, with the two conditions evaluated separately. This gap corresponds to research question RQ2 of Chapter 3.

Gap 3 (Req 3): The strongest multi-party mechanisms are those of Madine et al. [53], Tan et al. [69], Punia et al. [61], Zhao and Su [50], Maruthi and Singh [54] and Ekholm et al. [43], with partial mechanisms in Wu et al. [75], Hagström et al. [47], Al Amin et al. [38] and Abbasi et al. [35]. As set out above, the joint approval in these studies is contingent on the absence of the patient [53, 69, 54], reserved for particular request classes and bypassable in an emergency [61], placed among consumer-side delegates or institution-side investigators rather than patient-side parties [50, 75], or applied at consent registration rather than at each access decision [43, 47, 38]. None of the six mechanism classes is conjoined with a purpose or data-scope condition, and the two threshold gates that are formally proved [50, 54] are proved in isolation from any policy, temporal or lifecycle condition. What remains open is a verifiable threshold over a patient-defined approving set that is a standing component of the access-decision predicate and is evaluated on every request. This gap corresponds to research question RQ3 of Chapter 3.

Gap 4 (Req 4): The strongest policy enforcement is found in Eneh et al. [44], whose on-chain rules evaluate purpose, data category, sensitivity, jurisdiction and action with deny-by-default, in Panagoulias et al. [57], who verify a purpose conjunct over thousands of requests, in Román-Martínez et al. [63], Tith et al. [71], Albalwy et al. [37] and Jaiman and Urovi [49], who evaluate purpose against the consent, in the key-derivation scheme of [64], which binds role and consent into the key, and in Punia et al. [61], whose attribute policy is evaluated in a conjunctive predicate. In the remaining studies the policy is bound to the requester's role or attributes or to the ciphertext rather than to what the patient authorised [46, 56, 78, 36], the purpose is captured for audit but not adjudicated [72, 73], or the policy is described but not enforced [39, 41, 59]. Jurisdiction appears as a rule attribute only in Eneh et al. [44], and the declared purpose is never attested. What remains open is a purpose and data-scope policy that is bound to the consent object, evaluated together with the jurisdiction on every request, and conjoined with the multi-party approval condition. This gap corresponds to research question RQ4 of Chapter 3.

Gap 5 (Req 5): Temporal validity is enforced inside the decision by Eneh et al. [44], the scheme in [64], Madine et al. [53], Punia et al. [61] and Panagoulias et al. [57], credential or attribute expiry is enforced by Li et al. [51] and Mei et al. [55], and age windows are demonstrably enforced in the national portal studied by Hagström et al. [47]. Explicit lifecycle state machines are found in Phuyal et al. [58], Wu et al. [75] and Shanmugham and Senthilkumar [66], and verified revocation in Panagoulias et al. [57] and Phuyal et al. [58]. However, the enforced window is usually attached to a token, a key or a credential rather than to the consent [73, 51, 77], the stored expiry of the consent is not read by the decision [58], revocation does not invalidate tokens already issued [73], and no study verifies expiry, revocation and state transition together at the consent level in a multi-institution exchange. What remains open is the enforcement of the validity interval, immediate and verifiable revocation, and controlled transitions between lifecycle states of the consent object itself at every access decision. This gap corresponds to research question RQ5 of Chapter 3.

Gap 6 (Req 6): Formal proofs are provided by Wu and Zhang [76], Zhao and Su [50], Maruthi and Singh [54], Mei et al. [55], Hancheng et al. [48] and Luo et al. [52], in each case for a cryptographic property of a narrow predicate. Complete empirical evaluations are provided by Panagoulias et al. [57], Phuyal et al. [58], Albalwy et al. [37], Jaiman and Urovi [49] and Hagström et al. [47], and systematic adversarial testing without formal content by Tremper et al. [72] and Sawant and Gomes [65]. No study provides both, and the studies with the broadest predicates [61, 53, 45, 58, 66] provide neither a proof nor an ALLOW and DENY test of the decision. What remains open is the formal definition and proof of the properties of the conjoined predicate, namely identity correctness, authorisation integrity, threshold security, temporal safety and lifecycle safety, together with an empirical evaluation that demonstrates the refusal of the negative cases. This gap corresponds to research question RQ6 of Chapter 3.

This chapter has presented a systematic literature review, conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020, of the studies that address the authorisation of patient consent in decentralised healthcare data sharing. Six requirements for a trustworthy multi-party consent authorisation framework were defined in Section 2.2 and used as the basis of comparison throughout the chapter. Eight frozen searches across seven bibliographic databases, supplemented by a Google Scholar discovery arm, identified 9,256 records, of which 6,039 unique records were screened by title. After abstract screening, full-text assessment and quality appraisal, 44 primary studies published between 2020 and 2026 were retained, together with three secondary studies that were used as background only. The studies were reviewed in six streams corresponding to the six requirements, and each study was assessed against all six requirements in the tables of Section 2.4.

The review found that the individual conditions of a trustworthy authorisation decision are each represented in the literature. Evaluable consent objects have existed since 2020, purpose-based and attribute-based policy engines operate inside the decision in a number of systems, temporal validity and revocation are enforced at decision time in a few, identity and authority are separated most clearly where guardianship or professional licensing is verified against an external register or credential, and multi-party approval exists in six mechanism classes. The review also found that these conditions are not conjoined. Multi-party approval appears as a contingency path, a registration-time co-consent, an institution-side gate, a custodial threshold, a witness threshold or a key-share reconstruction rather than as a standing condition of every access decision; the purpose and data-scope policy is never conjoined with multi-party approval; temporal and lifecycle enforcement at the consent level is rarely verified; and formal assurance, where it exists, covers a narrow cryptographic predicate while the broadest predicates are neither proved nor tested. The research gap is therefore a conjunction gap and an assurance gap, as stated in Section 2.5 and decomposed by requirement in Section 2.5.1.

These two gaps define the research undertaken in the remainder of this report. The conjunction gap motivates a consent object whose components, namely the participating identities, the guardian set G and the threshold N, the purpose and data scope, the validity interval, the jurisdiction, the lifecycle state and the evidence, are evaluated as separate predicates whose conjunction determines every access decision. The assurance gap motivates the formal definition of the security properties of that conjunction and their empirical validation in the HALAH prototype. In this context, the six requirements of Section 2.2 and the six gaps of Section 2.5.1 correspond one to one to the six sub-research questions and the six research objectives that follow. Chapter 3 defines the key terms and states the research questions.
